opportunities.gap: The Opening Case (line 20) asserts the four candidate files' modified dates 'all read today because the file was opened (not edited) on each.' This is technically false on every mainstream OS: merely opening a file does not update its last-modified timestamp (only the access time, which most file managers do not display). The vivid scenario rests on an incorrect claim about how timestamps work, undermining the section's credibility on the exact domain it teaches.
opportunities.proposed_change: Reword so the timestamp clustering is realistic: the dates cluster because the student saved/duplicated all four the same evening (Save As, copy-paste, autosave), or because file managers show date-modified to the day so several same-day saves look identical. Drop the 'opened (not edited)' causal claim. Keep the punchline that modified date alone cannot disambiguate version. Suggested replacement sentence: 'The modified dates all read today because the student saved, duplicated, and re-exported all four during the same late-night session, so they cluster to the same day.'

sources.cite: Microsoft Learn / Win32 file times documentation (NTFS access vs. modified time)
sources.finding: The last-write (modified) time is updated only when the file is written, not when it is opened/read; only the last-access time tracks opens, and on Windows last-access updates are disabled by default (NtfsDisableLastAccessUpdate). Confirms that opening a file does not change the date-modified that file managers display.
